title: 'The Good-morrow' and the aubade
short: A morning greeting that turns the dawn-song (aubade) inside out: the lovers wake not to part but to a new life.
body: The aubade, a song of lovers parting at dawn, was a familiar lyric kind (compare Romeo and Juliet III.v). Donne's poem begins not with daybreak but with a question about the lovers' whole past, and the dawn it greets is a spiritual one: their 'waking soules' have only now come alive in love. The poem was first printed in 1633. Grierson found two distinct manuscript versions; the 1633 text, followed here ('countrey pleasures', 'snorted', 'one world', 'better'), he judged the racier and probably the earlier. The date is unknown; many critics associate it with the love poetry of the later 1590s.

title: by my troth
short: 'Upon my faith': a colloquial oath; 'troth' is the same word as 'truth', also used of the plighted faith of lovers.
body: The mild oath sets the conversational, surprised tone characteristic of Donne's openings. 'Troth' (a variant of 'truth') means good faith, and was the word for a promise of marriage ('to plight one's troth', OED). The oath therefore quietly anticipates the poem's claim of mutual fidelity, while its colloquial abruptness breaks with the smooth openings of Elizabethan sonnets. Compare the brusque first lines of 'The Canonization' and 'The Sunne Rising'.

title: wean'd ... suck'd
short: Before love the lovers were like infants at the breast; love is their weaning, their entry into maturity.
body: The speaker treats all earlier experience as infancy: not yet weaned, the lovers 'suck'd' on simple pleasures 'childishly'. The image makes their earlier affairs both innocent and contemptible, and their present love a kind of coming of age. The vocabulary of nursing also belongs to the poem's language of birth and waking. The questions are rhetorical: the speaker answers them himself in l. 5, 'T'was so'.

title: countrey pleasures
short: Rustic, unrefined pleasures; many editors also hear a bawdy pun, as in Hamlet's 'country matters'. Other manuscripts read 'childish pleasures seelily'.
body: On the surface the phrase means simple rural amusements, set against the sophistication of the lovers' present state. Modern editors have noted the possible sexual pun on the first syllable of 'country', exploited by Hamlet to Ophelia (Hamlet III.ii, 'country matters'). The reading is textual as well as interpretative: Grierson records that the other manuscript recension reads 'childish pleasures seelily' (that is, sillily), a tamer line. Readers who accept the pun see the stanza as dismissing earlier, purely physical affairs.

title: the seaven sleepers den
short: Seven young Christians of Ephesus walled up in a cave under the emperor Decius (c. 250) who slept, by legend, for about two centuries.
body: The legend of the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus tells how seven young men fled persecution under Decius, were sealed in a cave, and woke under the Christian emperor Theodosius II. It was spread in the West by Gregory of Tours and Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, and appears also in the Qur'an (Sura 18). The lovers ask whether their life before love was such a sleep. 'Snorted' (snored) is deliberately undignified; the alternative manuscript version reads 'slumbred'.

anchor: t'was but a dreame of thee
title: but a dreame of thee
short: All earlier beauties were mere shadows or foretastes of the beloved, as particulars are shadows of the Platonic Idea.
body: 'But this' means 'except for this love'; all other pleasures are mere fancies. The claim that every earlier beauty was only a dream of the present beloved draws loosely on Platonic thinking, in which earthly beauties are imperfect copies of one ideal form. It also returns to the poem's opposition between sleeping and waking: the earlier affairs belonged to the dream; this love is the waking. The stanza's last line is a hexameter, a longer close used at the end of each stanza.

title: Stanza form
short: Three seven-line stanzas rhyming ababccc, in pentameter with a final alexandrine (six-foot line).
body: Each stanza has four alternately rhymed lines followed by a rhyming triplet; the closing line is lengthened to six stresses (an alexandrine), giving each stanza a weighty conclusion: 'a dreame of thee', 'each hath one, and is one', 'none can die'. The three stanzas move from past (what were we?), to present (good morrow), to future (can our love die?).

title: our waking soules
short: The lovers' souls are newly awake, and they watch each other with love rather than with jealous suspicion.
body: The greeting is addressed to the lovers' souls, not their bodies: the waking is spiritual. In l. 9 they 'watch' each other, but not as jealous lovers do, 'out of feare' of infidelity. The line alludes to the common Elizabethan figure of the suspicious lover keeping watch, and claims a love secure enough to be free of jealousy. Compare 'The Sunne Rising', where the lovers are spied on by the sun itself.

anchor: one little roome, an every where
title: one little roome, an every where
short: Love makes a small room a whole world: the microcosm-macrocosm idea that runs through Donne's love poems.
body: Love governs ('controules') all desire to look at anything else, and so makes the lovers' room contain everything. The idea of the lovers as a world complete in itself recurs in 'The Sunne Rising' ('This bed thy center is, these walls, thy spheare') and 'The Canonization'. 'An every where' turns an adverb into a noun, a characteristic compression. Behind it lies the Renaissance commonplace of man as a little world, a microcosm, mirroring the great world.

title: sea-discoverers to new worlds
short: The age of exploration: voyages to the Americas and beyond, in which Donne's own generation took part.
body: The late sixteenth century was the age of Drake's circumnavigation (1577-80) and Ralegh's Guiana voyage (1595); Donne himself sailed on the Cadiz (1596) and Azores (1597) expeditions. 'Let' is concessive: let others go discovering. The lovers' world is preferred to the new worlds of the explorers, as in 'The Sunne Rising', where the lovers outshine 'both th'India's of spice and Myne'. Carey has stressed Donne's fascination with expansion and possession; here the imperial vocabulary is turned into a claim of private sufficiency.

title: Let Maps to other, worlds on worlds have showne
short: Maps (perhaps 'map', 'mapps' or celestial charts) show others world after world; Grierson discusses the plural spelling.
body: The line can mean that maps have shown other people one world after another, or that celestial maps show worlds beyond worlds (new stars and the spheres of the cosmos). Grierson notes that the 1633 printing may have dropped an 's' which most manuscripts give, and that a plural without 's' was still common. The comma after 'other' in this text makes 'to other' mean 'to other people'. Either way the line extends l. 12: explorers and cartographers multiply worlds; the lovers need only one.

anchor: each hath one, and is one
title: each hath one, and is one
short: Each lover possesses a world (the other) and is a world (to the other); the two make one shared world.
body: The line compresses the stanza's argument: the lovers together 'possesse one world', yet each also 'hath one' (the beloved) and 'is one' (a world to the other). The other manuscript recension reads 'our world', which Grierson thought less characteristic. Critics disagree whether the line emphasises union (two in one) or a delicate balance of two separate worlds; the ambiguity prepares for the final stanza, where the lovers are two hemispheres of a single globe.

title: My face in thine eye
short: Each lover sees his or her own reflection in the other's eye: a common Renaissance love-image.
body: Gazing closely, each lover sees a tiny reflection of his or her face in the other's pupil, an image popularly called 'looking babies'. Donne uses it again in 'The Extasie' ('pictures in our eyes to get') and 'Witchcraft by a Picture'. The faces show 'true plaine hearts': honest, unconcealing, because the face is the mirror of the heart. The eyes thus become the 'hemispheares' of the next lines.

title: two better hemispheares
short: The lovers' faces (or eyes) are two half-globes making a perfect world, without the cold north or the declining west.
body: The faces, or the reflecting eyes, are two hemispheres, the halves of the lovers' one world. Unlike the real globe, this world has no 'sharpe North' (cold, bitter) and no 'declining West' (where the sun sets, and so decline and death). The other recension reads 'fitter' for 'better'; Grierson argued that Donne means each is a whole and better world to the other, not merely that they fit together. The cosmic and geographical images of stanza 2 are thus brought down to the lovers' faces.

title: What ever dyes, was not mixt equally
greek: Latin 'non enim invenitur corruptio nisi ubi invenitur contrarietas'
short: Scholastic physics: things decay because their elements are unequally mixed and contrary; a perfectly balanced compound cannot dissolve.
body: Grierson glosses this from Aquinas, who argues (on the incorruptibility of the soul) that corruption occurs only where there is contrariety: a simple substance, or a compound without contrary elements, cannot perish. In Galenic medicine also, death followed imbalance among the four humours. The lovers' love, if perfectly mixed, or if the two loves are 'one', should therefore be immortal. Grierson also compares a sermon in which Donne argues for the immortality of resurrected bodies.

title: If ... none can die
short: The poem ends on a condition, not a certainty: the lovers are immortal only if their loves are one or perfectly matched.
body: The last two lines offer alternatives: either the two loves are one, or the lovers love so alike that neither slackens. 'Die' carries its usual Elizabethan pun on sexual climax, so the line can also mean that love will never be spent. Critics divide on the tone: some hear triumphant assurance, others an anxious 'if' that admits love's mortality. Gardner and later editors note that the whole argument depends on the scholastic premise of l. 19.

title: The two versions of the poem
short: The poem survives in two manuscript recensions; this text follows the 1633 version.
body: Grierson found that the manuscripts give two distinct recensions. The 1633 edition and a few manuscripts read 'countrey pleasures childishly', 'snorted', 'one world' and 'better'; the more common version reads 'childish pleasures seelily', 'slumbred', 'our world' and 'fitter'. Grierson preferred the 1633 text as more vigorous and probably earlier; Gardner and later editors debate which represents Donne's revision. The variants show that Donne's lyrics circulated in manuscript, and were likely revised, long before they were printed.
